statements.status_notes: A time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition in the dynamic loader (ld.so) of the GNU C Library (glibc) versions 2.14 through 2.44 allows a local attacker to escalate privileges. When expanding $ORIGIN in DT_RPATH for setuid/setgid (AT_SECURE) programs, glibc validates the lexically normalized search path against the trusted directories but then opens the raw, un-normalized path. On systems where fs.protected_hardlinks is disabled, an attacker who hard-links such a program and swaps a path component for a symbolic link can make the loader load an attacker-controlled shared object.
statements.impact_statement: Exploitation needs a setuid or setgid binary whose DT_RPATH uses $ORIGIN, plus a local attacker able to hard-link it and win a race. None of the setuid/setgid binaries shipped in the Liquibase Secure image (su, passwd, mount, chsh and the other shadow and util-linux tools) contain $ORIGIN at all, and the container runs Liquibase as the unprivileged liquibase user. fs.protected_hardlinks, enabled by default on major distributions, also blocks the hard-link step.

statements.status_notes: In Bouncy Castle for Java before 1.85, Name Constraints bypass via trailing dot in rfc822Name and URI. This issue also affects Bouncy Castle for Java LTS before 2.73.12, and Bouncy Castle for Java FIPS (BC-FJA) before bc-fips 1.0.2.7 (1.0.X series), 2.0.2 (2.0.X series) and 2.1.3 (2.1.X series).
statements.impact_statement: This affected bcprov-jdk18on before 1.85. This repository now ships org.bouncycastle:bcprov-jdk18on:1.85, past the fixed version, as defense-in-depth. Independent of version, a source review found zero direct `import org.bouncycastle.` usage anywhere in this codebase, and zero references to NameConstraints, rfc822Name, GeneralSubtree, or PKIXNameConstraintValidator. The only Bouncy Castle usage in production code is Snowflake private-key loading through a shaded `net.snowflake.client.jdbc.internal.org.bouncycastle.*` namespace — a different package entirely from the standalone bcprov-jdk18on artifact this CVE affects, and one that never exercises certificate name-constraint validation.

statements.status_notes: The nscd service in the GNU C Library 2.3.4 onwards may crash due to a stack overflow when a malicious DNS server returns too large a response for a DNS query, resulting in degraded DNS resolution for the system. Exploitation of this bug needs a system that has nscd enabled and using an untrusted DNS server for name resolution, with the compromised DNS server being capable of processing records large enough to result in a stack overflow in an nscd thread stack. During experimentation, bind 9 was unable to handle large records, but that could change in future or with a different name server. In typical installations, nscd is executed in an isolated context as its own user without a shell, due to which any compromise of that service is isolated. There is a remote possibility of nscd cache corruption if an attacker manages to get the stack pointer into a desired point in the heap, potentially resulting in other caches in nscd being overwritten with corrupt data through the stack overflow, until the buggy code path eventually results in a crash. Finally, a crash in nscd may result in performance degradation when resolving names, but it does not result in a denial of service.
statements.impact_statement: glibc nscd stack-overflow crash when a malicious DNS server returns an oversized response. Requires nscd running against an untrusted DNS server; this minimal image runs no nscd process at all.

statements.status_notes: PCRE2 before 10.48 has a pcre2_match out-of-bounds read after a JIT fallback when an attacker can provide invalid UTF data.
statements.impact_statement: PCRE2 pcre2_match out-of-bounds read after a JIT fallback on invalid UTF data, fixed upstream in PCRE2 10.48 but not yet backported to Ubuntu noble. Liquibase is a pure-Java application (java.util.regex) with no linkage to native libpcre2, and docker-entrypoint.sh performs no regex or grep operations.

statements.status_notes: A flaw in curl's cookie parsing logic allows a malicious HTTP server to set "super cookies" that bypass the Public Suffix List check. This enables an attacker-controlled origin to inject cookies that curl subsequently scopes and transmits to unrelated third-party domains.
statements.impact_statement: The scanned image reports curl 7.81.0-1ubuntu1.20, below Ubuntu's fixed 7.81.0-1ubuntu1.25, but this issue requires Liquibase Secure to act as a curl HTTP client that parses and stores attacker-controlled cookies and later reuses them against unrelated domains. Liquibase Secure's build downloads use wget, and its stock runtime path invokes Liquibase rather than curl, so curl's cookie parsing, Public Suffix List, and cookie jar handling are not exercised.

statements.status_notes: The curl logic that works with SASL authentication could end up cleaning up the GSASL context twice without clearing the pointer in between, making it free() the same pointer twice.
statements.impact_statement: This CVE requires a libcurl-based application to use SASL authentication and exercise the GSASL cleanup path on a curl handle. Liquibase Secure's stock container does not invoke curl for its own build or runtime operations, and a source review found no references to GSASL, SASL-authenticated curl flows, or libcurl option usage in the product runtime path. curl is inherited from the base image only, so the vulnerable libcurl path is not reachable from Liquibase Secure.

statements.status_notes: When reusing a libcurl handle for sequential transfers driven by environment-variable proxy configuration, libcurl fails to clear the proxy authentication state between requests. Specifically, if the initial transfer authenticates against proxyA using Digest auth, a subsequent transfer routed through proxyB erroneously leaks the Proxy-Authorization header intended solely for proxyA.
statements.impact_statement: This CVE requires a libcurl-based application to reuse a handle across sequential transfers that pick up proxy settings from environment variables and negotiate Digest authentication to multiple proxies. Liquibase Secure's stock container does not invoke curl for its own build or runtime operations, and a source review found no references to proxy-authenticated libcurl flows or related curl option usage in the product runtime path. curl is inherited from the base image only, so the vulnerable libcurl path is not reachable from Liquibase Secure.

statements.status_notes: libcurl would reuse a previously created connection even when some mTLS config related option had been changed that should have prohibited reuse. libcurl keeps previously used connections in a connection pool for subsequent transfers to reuse if one of them matches the setup. However, some TLS settings related to client certificates were left out from the configuration match checks, making them match too easily. In particular options related to the private key.
statements.impact_statement: This CVE requires a libcurl-based application to reuse pooled connections while changing mutual-TLS client-certificate settings. Liquibase Secure's stock container does not invoke curl for its own build or runtime operations, and a source review found no references to libcurl mutual-TLS option usage or connection-pool handling in the product runtime path. curl is inherited from the base image only, so the vulnerable libcurl path is not reachable from Liquibase Secure.

statements.status_notes: NumberInput.looksLikeValidNumber() in FasterXML jackson-core pre-validates stringified numbers with two regular expressions: PATTERN_FLOAT, present since 2.17.0, and PATTERN_FLOAT_TRAILING_DOT, added in 2.17.2. PATTERN_FLOAT places adjacent quantifiers over the same character class so input that ultimately fails to match forces Java's backtracking engine to retry every possible split point of the digit run. Matching cost therefore grows with the square of the input length. An attacker who can supply JSON that an application deserializes into a numeric target type reaches this method through jackson-databind's default String-to-number coercion for BigDecimal, BigInteger, Double and Float, and a small number of concurrent requests can exhaust a server's request-handling thread pool. The fix replaces both regular expressions with a hand-rolled single-pass scan.
statements.impact_statement: Fixed in jackson-core 2.18.11, 2.21.7 and 2.22.3. Every published Liquibase Secure image from 5.0.0 through 6.0.0 carries in-range copies, so this assessment does not rest on version. The copies were read from the version class of each copy in the shipped jars, including the obfuscated copy inside the core Liquibase Secure jar and copies relocated inside vendor drivers. In 6.0.0 the first-party copies are 2.22.2, the Couchbase SDK copy is 2.21.6, the snowflake-jdbc copy is 2.18.10 and the databricks-jdbc copy is 2.18.8; earlier releases carry older in-range copies. The vulnerable regular expression runs only when jackson-databind coerces a JSON string into a Float, Double, Number or BigDecimal target. A bytecode scan of every shipped jar found looksLikeValidNumber() called only by those jackson-databind number deserializers. Every Jackson binding call in Liquibase Secure's own code, including the changelog, snapshot, import-file, checks and license parsers, targets JsonNode trees, Object, Map or List of Map, where JSON strings stay strings and are never coerced. The license-tracking application in the 5.x ZIP binds request bodies whose fields are strings, string maps, whole numbers, booleans and dates only. The relocated vendor copies are private to their drivers and parse responses from the database service.

statements.status_notes: UTF8DataInputJsonParser._reportInvalidToken() in FasterXML jackson-core builds the offending-token text for its error message by appending Java identifier characters to a StringBuilder in a loop that has no upper bound. Unlike sibling parser implementations, it never consults ErrorReportConfiguration.getMaxErrorTokenLength(). A malformed token supplied to a parser created through JsonFactory.createParser(DataInput) is therefore accumulated in full, which can drive the StringBuilder to many times the raw payload size and trigger OutOfMemoryError for the JVM. Releases before 2.8.0 do not contain the affected class.
statements.impact_statement: Fixed in jackson-core 2.18.11, 2.21.7 and 2.22.3. Every published Liquibase Secure image from 5.0.0 through 6.0.0 carries in-range copies, so this assessment does not rest on version. The copies were read from the version class of each copy in the shipped jars, including the obfuscated copy inside the core Liquibase Secure jar and copies relocated inside vendor drivers. In 6.0.0 the first-party copies are 2.22.2, the Couchbase SDK copy is 2.21.6, the snowflake-jdbc copy is 2.18.10 and the databricks-jdbc copy is 2.18.8; earlier releases carry older in-range copies. The unbounded error-token buffer is in UTF8DataInputJsonParser, which Jackson creates only for input supplied as a java.io.DataInput through createParser(DataInput), readValue(DataInput) or readTree(DataInput). A bytecode scan of every class in every shipped jar, first-party and vendor, including the license-tracking application in the 5.x ZIP, found no code outside Jackson itself that passes a DataInput to Jackson. Liquibase Secure parses JSON from streams, readers, strings and files, which use the other parser implementations that do enforce the error-token limit.

statements.status_notes: UTF8DataInputJsonParser._reportInvalidToken() in jackson-core builds the offending-token text for its error message by appending Java identifier characters to a StringBuilder in a loop that has no upper bound and never consults the configured maximum error-token length. A malformed token supplied to a parser created from a DataInput is therefore accumulated in full, which can exhaust the JVM heap.
statements.impact_statement: Fixed in tools.jackson.core jackson-core 3.1.7 and 3.2.3. Liquibase Secure 6.0.0 carries one Jackson 3 copy, 3.2.2, inside the Cassandra extension, where it is used by the bundled Cassandra driver. The license-tracking application in the 5.1.x and 5.2.x ZIP also carries Jackson 3 copies inside the advisory range. Earlier images carry no Jackson 3. The unbounded error-token buffer is in UTF8DataInputJsonParser, which Jackson creates only for input supplied as a java.io.DataInput. A bytecode scan of every class in every shipped jar, the Cassandra extension and the license-tracking application included, found no code outside Jackson itself that passes a DataInput to Jackson, so the parser with the unbounded buffer is never created.

statements.status_notes: Issue summary: When CMS password-based decryption (RFC 3211 / PWRI key unwrap) processes attacker-supplied CMS data, an attacker-chosen stream-mode KEK cipher can trigger a heap out-of-bounds read in kek_unwrap_key(). Impact summary: A heap buffer over-read may trigger a crash which leads to Denial of Service for an application if the input buffer ends at a memory page boundary and the following page is unmapped. There is no information disclosure as the over-read bytes are not revealed to the attacker.
statements.impact_statement: This CVE affects OpenSSL CMS password-based decryption when attacker-supplied CMS data reaches CMS_decrypt() or CMS_decrypt_set1_password(). Liquibase Secure's stock container runs the Liquibase Java CLI rather than OpenSSL CMS tooling, and a source review found no references to CMS_decrypt, CMS_decrypt_set1_password, PWRI key unwrapping, S/MIME, or PKCS#7 processing in the product runtime path. libssl3 is inherited from the base image only, so the vulnerable CMS decryption path is not reachable from Liquibase Secure.

statements.status_notes: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature vulnerability in dashbit nimble_zta allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to authenticate as an arbitrary Cloudflare service token. Applications using the Cloudflare Zero Trust authentication strategy are affected. This issue affects nimble_zta from 0.1.2 before 0.1.3.
statements.impact_statement: False match. The CVE is for nimble_zta, an Elixir authentication library published by dashbit, not for the dash shell. The Ubuntu tracker attributes it to the dash package by name. The Liquibase Secure image ships no Elixir or Erlang runtime and no nimble_zta code.

statements.status_notes: TypeDeserializerBase._findDeserializer() in FasterXML jackson-databind caches the resolved deserializer under the raw, attacker-supplied type ID. When name-based polymorphism is configured with a fallback, for example @JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.NAME, defaultImpl = ...), every distinct unrecognized type ID resolves to the same fallback deserializer but is retained as its own key in the _deserializers map. That map has no configurable bound and lives for the lifetime of the type deserializer, so an attacker who can repeatedly supply fresh unknown type IDs causes monotonic memory retention across requests. Exploitation requires an application that enables name-based polymorphism with a defaultImpl or equivalent fallback, accepts attacker-influenced type IDs, and reuses a long-lived ObjectMapper across requests. This affects tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind from 3.0.0 through 3.1.6 and from 3.2.0 through 3.2.2. Users should upgrade to 3.1.7 or 3.2.3.
statements.impact_statement: Fixed in tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind 3.1.7 and 3.2.3. The 6.0.0 image is the only published Liquibase Secure image that ships Jackson 3: one copy at 3.2.2, inside liquibase-commercial-cassandra, read from its PackageVersion class. The 5.x images ship no Jackson 3 at all. 3.2.2 is inside the advisory range, so this assessment does not rest on version. The vulnerable cache is filled only through name-based polymorphic typing with a fallback, such as @JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.NAME, defaultImpl = ...), applied to attacker-chosen type IDs. A scan of every class in that jar, the Cassandra driver and JDBC wrapper included, found no @JsonTypeInfo, @JsonSubTypes or default typing. Liquibase's own code does not use Jackson 3. With no polymorphic type handling configured for Jackson 3, no type-ID cache is ever created.

statements.status_notes: TypeDeserializerBase._findDeserializer() in jackson-databind caches the resolved deserializer under the raw, attacker-supplied type ID. When name-based polymorphism is configured with a fallback, for example @JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.NAME, defaultImpl = ...), every distinct unrecognized type ID resolves to the same fallback deserializer but is retained as its own key in an unbounded, process-lifetime map, so an attacker who can repeatedly supply fresh unknown type IDs causes monotonic memory retention. This affects com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind from 2.0.0 through 2.18.10, from 2.19.0 through 2.21.6, and from 2.22.0 through 2.22.2. Users should upgrade to 2.18.11, 2.21.7 or 2.22.3.
statements.impact_statement: The same advisory covers the Jackson 2 coordinate, which is a separate artifact with its own version line. Fixed in jackson-databind 2.18.11, 2.21.7 and 2.22.3. Every published Liquibase Secure image from 5.0.0 through 6.0.0 carries only copies inside the advisory range. In 6.0.0 those are the first-party 2.22.2 and the copies relocated inside the Couchbase SDK (2.21.6), databricks-jdbc (2.18.8) and snowflake-jdbc (2.18.10), read from the PackageVersion class in each jar. So this assessment does not rest on version. The vulnerable cache is filled only through name-based polymorphic typing with a fallback, such as @JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.NAME, defaultImpl = ...), applied to attacker-chosen type IDs. A scan of every class in every shipped jar found no @JsonTypeInfo and no default typing in any Liquibase code. Three vendor libraries declare it. Apache Arrow's ArrowType, bundled with the BigQuery, Databricks and Snowflake drivers, uses name-based typing with no fallback, so an unknown type ID fails instead of being cached. The Couchbase SDK's bucket configuration type also has no fallback. The Couchbase SDK's analytics link model does declare a fallback. It is read only by the SDK's analytics link management API, which Liquibase never calls, and its input would be a Couchbase server response rather than user input.

statements.status_notes: Forward-reference completion for @JsonIdentityInfo object IDs in FasterXML jackson-databind performs a linear scan of the pending-reference accumulator for every resolved ID. The affected paths are CollectionDeserializer.CollectionReferringAccumulator. resolveForwardReference() and the equivalent implementation in MapDeserializer. When a document first creates N unresolved object-ID references in an identity-enabled collection or map and then defines those same IDs in reverse order, completion performs on the order of N * (N + 1) / 2 identity comparisons, so a shallow document whose size grows linearly causes quadratic CPU work during deserialization. Exploitation requires an application that deserializes attacker-influenced JSON into an identity-enabled collection or map. This affects tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind from 3.0.0 through 3.1.6 and from 3.2.0 through 3.2.2. Users should upgrade to 3.1.7 or 3.2.3.
statements.impact_statement: Fixed in tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind 3.1.7 and 3.2.3. The 6.0.0 image is the only published Liquibase Secure image that ships Jackson 3: one copy at 3.2.2, inside liquibase-commercial-cassandra, read from its PackageVersion class. The 5.x images ship no Jackson 3 at all. 3.2.2 is inside the advisory range, so this assessment does not rest on version. The quadratic lookup runs only when JSON is deserialized into a collection or map of @JsonIdentityInfo-enabled values. A scan of every class in that jar, the Cassandra driver and JDBC wrapper included, found no @JsonIdentityInfo or Jackson object-ID generator. Liquibase's own code does not use Jackson 3. With no object identity configured, the forward-reference accumulator is never created.

statements.status_notes: Forward-reference completion for @JsonIdentityInfo object IDs in jackson-databind performs a linear scan of the pending-reference accumulator for every resolved ID, in CollectionDeserializer.CollectionReferringAccumulator.resolveForwardReference() and the equivalent map implementation. A shallow document that creates N unresolved references and then defines them in reverse order causes quadratic CPU work. This affects com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind from 2.5.0 through 2.18.10, from 2.19.0 through 2.21.6, and from 2.22.0 through 2.22.2. Users should upgrade to 2.18.11, 2.21.7 or 2.22.3.

statements.status_notes: Expat through 2.8.4 fails to validate low surrogates following high surrogates in UTF-16 input, allowing malformed UTF-16 sequences to be accepted. Attackers can craft UTF-16 encoded XML with lone high surrogates that consume following code units, hiding markup characters from the parser and enabling XML injection attacks.
statements.impact_statement: Expat UTF-16 surrogate-pair validation issue allowing malformed XML to be accepted. Liquibase's changelog XML parsing uses the JDK-bundled JAXP/Xerces parser (pure Java) and never links the native libexpat library. The embedded GraalPy runtime used by liquibase-checks does not use xml/pyexpat in its default pipeline.

statements.status_notes: Archive::Tar versions before 3.10 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via an attacker-controlled entry size field in a tar header. A crafted header declaring a multi-gigabyte size causes Perl to allocate a scalar of that size.
statements.impact_statement: Scanner package misattribution. The vulnerable code is the Archive::Tar module, which Ubuntu ships in perl-modules, not in perl-base. perl-modules is not installed in any Liquibase Secure image: perl-base carries only the interpreter and a minimal core module set, there is no Archive/Tar.pm anywhere on the image, and loading Archive::Tar fails with "Can't locate Archive/Tar.pm". The scanner matched a fix in the perl source package to perl-base, which does not contain the vulnerable module. Even setting that aside, nothing in the runtime path executes perl. Ubuntu fixes this in perl 5.38.2-3.2ubuntu0.4 (noble); jammy has no fix yet.

statements.status_notes: When a libcurl-based application performs transfers via SCP:// or SFTP:// and utilizes the CURLOPT_SSH_KEYFUNCTION callback, it may silently accept an untrusted server. This vulnerability occurs when a server presents a host key type that does not match the specific key type already recorded for that host in the known_hosts file. Instead of rejecting the mismatch, the callback mechanism fails to properly enforce the restriction, allowing the connection to succeed without warning and risking a potential man-in-the-middle attack.
statements.impact_statement: This CVE requires a libcurl-based application to perform SCP or SFTP transfers and register the CURLOPT_SSH_KEYFUNCTION callback so host-key validation flows through the vulnerable known_hosts handling. Liquibase Secure's stock container does not invoke curl for its own build or runtime operations, and a source review found no references to SCP, SFTP, CURLOPT_SSH_KEYFUNCTION, or known_hosts callback handling in the product runtime path. curl is inherited from the base image only, so the vulnerable libcurl path is not reachable from Liquibase Secure.

statements.status_notes: A stack-based buffer overflow in the dynamic loader (ld.so) of the GNU C Library (glibc) versions 2.14 through 2.44 allows a local attacker to crash or corrupt the memory of setuid/setgid (AT_SECURE) programs. When such a program's DT_RPATH or DT_RUNPATH begins with $ORIGIN and is followed by NUL or '/', the loader reads past the end of the path buffer and writes past the end of a stack-allocated internal buffer.
statements.impact_statement: Exploitation needs a setuid or setgid binary whose DT_RPATH or DT_RUNPATH begins with $ORIGIN. None of the setuid/setgid binaries shipped in the Liquibase Secure image (su, passwd, mount, chsh and the other shadow and util-linux tools) contain $ORIGIN at all, and the container runs Liquibase as the unprivileged liquibase user.

statements.status_notes: urllib3 is an HTTP client library for Python. From 1.26.0 until 2.8.0, the proxy_ssl_context, proxy_assert_hostname, proxy_assert_fingerprint, ssl_context, cert_reqs, verify_mode, use_forwarding_for_https=True, and CERT_NONE configuration paths fail to remain separated because target-server TLS settings are incorrectly applied to the HTTPS proxy connection. Applying cert_reqs=CERT_NONE can overwrite proxy_ssl_context.verify_mode in place, and the mutation persists so later connections reusing the same context may connect to the HTTPS proxy without certificate verification. An attacker who intercepts and impersonates the HTTPS proxy can then observe or modify forwarded traffic or receive a target TLS client certificate. This issue is fixed in version 2.8.0.
statements.impact_statement: urllib3 ships only inside the Python virtual environment embedded in the checks extension's GraalPy scripting engine; the image has no system Python and no other copy. None of the check scripts Liquibase bundles and runs by default import urllib3, and no other bundled Python package depends on it. The HTTPS-proxy TLS-setting confusion is only reached when Python code sends HTTPS requests through an HTTPS proxy with target-specific TLS settings, which requires a customer to author and configure their own custom check script that does so; no shipped configuration does this out of the box. From Liquibase Secure 5.2.0 the embedded Python engine also denies scripts host socket access unless liquibase.script.python.allowHostAccess is enabled. Liquibase Secure 5.0.0 through 5.0.2 bundle urllib3 1.26.15, 5.0.3 bundles 1.26.18, 5.1.0 bundles no standalone urllib3, 5.1.1 bundles 2.6.3, and 5.2.0 through 5.2.2 bundle 2.7.0, all inside the affected range; 5.0.0 through 5.1.1 also carry urllib3 1.26.16 vendored inside pip, a build-time installer that nothing imports at runtime and that 5.2.0 removed. Liquibase Secure 6.0.0 bundles urllib3 2.8.0, which includes the fix.

statements.status_notes: urllib3 is an HTTP client library for Python. From 2.6.2 until 2.8.0, HTTPResponse.stream and HTTPResponse.read_chunked can enter an infinite loop because the Deflate decoder retains trailing bytes as unconsumed input after reaching end-of-stream and repeatedly decodes them without progress. The issue occurs when an untrusted server sends a chunked Deflate response whose decoded body exceeds a positive finite chunk size and whose encoded body has trailing bytes. The impact is excessive CPU usage and a request that does not complete, and network read timeouts do not interrupt the loop because no further socket read occurs. This issue is fixed in version 2.8.0.
statements.impact_statement: urllib3 ships only inside the Python virtual environment embedded in the checks extension's GraalPy scripting engine; the image has no system Python and no other copy. None of the check scripts Liquibase bundles and runs by default import urllib3, and no other bundled Python package depends on it. The Deflate decoder infinite loop is only reached when Python code streams a chunked, Deflate-encoded HTTP response from a malicious server, which requires a customer to author and configure their own custom check script that does so; no shipped configuration does this out of the box. From Liquibase Secure 5.2.0 the embedded Python engine also denies scripts host socket access unless liquibase.script.python.allowHostAccess is enabled. Only Liquibase Secure 5.1.1 (urllib3 2.6.3) and 5.2.0 through 5.2.2 (urllib3 2.7.0) bundle a version inside the affected range; 5.0.0 through 5.0.3 bundle urllib3 1.26.15 or 1.26.18, which predate the vulnerable code, 5.1.0 bundles no standalone urllib3, and the urllib3 1.26.16 vendored inside pip in 5.0.0 through 5.1.1 is also outside the range. Liquibase Secure 6.0.0 bundles urllib3 2.8.0, which includes the fix.

statements.status_notes: urllib3 is an HTTP client library for Python. From 1.10.3 until 2.8.0, the HTTPResponse.read_chunked and HTTPResponse.stream methods can allocate unbounded memory because the streaming chunk parser buffers the chunk-size field until newline or EOF without a length bound. A malicious server that returns Transfer-Encoding: chunked followed by a very long run of bytes without a newline can exhaust the client process's memory. This issue is fixed in version 2.8.0.
statements.impact_statement: urllib3 ships only inside the Python virtual environment embedded in the checks extension's GraalPy scripting engine; the image has no system Python and no other copy. None of the check scripts Liquibase bundles and runs by default import urllib3, and no other bundled Python package depends on it. The unbounded chunk-size buffering is only reached when Python code reads a chunked HTTP response from a malicious server, which requires a customer to author and configure their own custom check script that does so; no shipped configuration does this out of the box. From Liquibase Secure 5.2.0 the embedded Python engine also denies scripts host socket access unless liquibase.script.python.allowHostAccess is enabled. Liquibase Secure 5.0.0 through 5.0.2 bundle urllib3 1.26.15, 5.0.3 bundles 1.26.18, 5.1.0 bundles no standalone urllib3, 5.1.1 bundles 2.6.3, and 5.2.0 through 5.2.2 bundle 2.7.0, all inside the affected range; 5.0.0 through 5.1.1 also carry urllib3 1.26.16 vendored inside pip, a build-time installer that nothing imports at runtime and that 5.2.0 removed. Liquibase Secure 6.0.0 bundles urllib3 2.8.0, which includes the fix.

statements.status_notes: sqlparse: formatting a list of tuples leads to denial of service. Formatting a long list of tuples with sqlparse hangs, causing excessive CPU consumption. Fixed in 0.5.4.
statements.impact_statement: sqlparse ships in the runtime virtual environment of the checks module's embedded Python scripting engine, which end users can use to author custom check scripts; the build only strips pip, setuptools, and their installer machinery from that environment, not sqlparse itself. None of the check scripts Liquibase bundles and runs by default import sqlparse — they use a different SQL parsing library for changeset SQL. This advisory's vulnerable tuple-list formatting code path is only reachable if a customer authors and configures their own custom check script that imports sqlparse and formats attacker-influenced SQL with it; no shipped configuration does this out of the box.

statements.status_notes: Jackson Core 3.x maxNestingDepth constraint bypass in multiple parser implementations, enabling DoS via StackOverflowError from deeply nested JSON input.
statements.impact_statement: Repo-wide searches found no source declaration for tools.jackson.core:jackson-core. The build only references com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-core 2.22.1 at pom.xml:57,150-151, community-extensions/liquibase-mongodb/pom.xml:48,90-92, and core/liquibase-dist/src/main/archive/licenses/commercial/README.txt:137. The scanner-reported 3.1.0 coordinate is not present in the codebase.

statements.status_notes: Memory leak in Netty's DNS codec when processing malicious DNS response packets containing invalid domain names. The record decoder fails to release allocated ByteBuf resources before the IDNA-validation exception is thrown, allowing incremental memory exhaustion through sustained malicious DNS responses.
statements.impact_statement: Netty's DNS record decoder fails to release allocated ByteBuf resources before throwing on domain names that violate IDNA rules, leaking memory per malformed record. Unlike the server-side Netty DNS codec findings above, this path is reached during Liquibase's own outbound DNS resolution, but only triggers when the DNS server answering that resolution (or an on-path attacker able to forge responses) returns malformed records. This requires a compromised or malicious DNS resolution path — an attacker already in a position to forge DNS responses to Liquibase's outbound queries could achieve more direct impact (e.g. redirecting database connections) than a gradual memory leak. No CVE has been assigned to this advisory at the time of assessment. Netty is a transitive dependency from Azure SDK, Cassandra driver, and MongoDB driver — used only as a client-side transport for outbound connections.

statements.status_notes: Jackson Core's async parser can accumulate excessively long digit sequences (~20,000x amplification of the intended maxNumberLength limit) when input is fed in small chunks without a terminator, weakening DoS protection for applications that rely on maxNumberLength.
statements.impact_statement: Incomplete fix for a prior number-length constraint bypass: Jackson's async/non-blocking parser (NonBlockingJsonParser / ByteArrayFeeder) silently buffers digit characters up to maxStringLength instead of enforcing maxNumberLength when input arrives in small chunks without a terminator byte. Found in jackson-core 2.22.0 bundled into liquibase-aws-extension.jar and liquibase-azure.jar. Both extensions are outbound clients that call AWS/Azure APIs and parse the responses those services return over TLS; neither extension's own code invokes Jackson's non-blocking parser API, and neither exposes a network-facing endpoint that accepts attacker-controlled JSON. Exploiting this would require an attacker already able to forge or MITM AWS/Azure API responses, at which point far more direct attacks are already available.

crypto/x509 name-constraint quadratic behavior is not reachable in the Liquibase Secure container. The secure Docker image installs lpm from a release ZIP (core/docker/Dockerfile:39) and the runtime entrypoint only uses lpm to add mysql when INSTALL_MYSQL is set (core/docker/docker-entrypoint.sh:4). A repo-wide search found no code path that parses attacker-controlled certificate chains or invokes the affected x509 name-constraint APIs at runtime.

encoding/pem quadratic parsing behavior is not reachable in the Liquibase Secure container. The secure Docker image installs lpm from a release ZIP (core/docker/Dockerfile:39) and the runtime entrypoint only uses lpm to add mysql when INSTALL_MYSQL is set (core/docker/docker-entrypoint.sh: 4). A repo-wide search found no code path that parses untrusted PEM input at runtime.

Current Liquibase Secure Docker builds install lpm 0.3.5 (docker/Dockerfile:35), and the upstream liquibase-package-manager v0.3.5 go.mod declares go 1.25.11 (liquibase-package-manager/go.mod:3), which is newer than the scanner-reported Go 1.25.1 and includes the fix. GitHub code search for liquibase/liquibase-package-manager found no crypto/x509 imports or references, so the vulnerable certificate-chain path is not exercised by lpm source.
